summary:
Wrote the course blueprint for dewsharp. Files: /home/user/dewsharp/planning/COURSE_MAP.md (new, 1,330 lines), /home/user/dewsharp/courses/pdp.yaml and /home/user/dewsharp/courses/foop.yaml (new drafts in the LESSON_FORMAT "Courses" shape), and /home/user/dewsharp/DECISIONS.md (entries 9 to 15 appended). I did not write any lessons or repo code, and did not commit.

**The plan.**
- **PDP:** 26 lessons and 3 mixed sets, in three series. dewlab's Programming Foundations is split in two ("First programs"; "Methods, lists and algorithms"), and "Working in a team" is kept.
- **FOOP:** 21 lessons and 3 mixed sets. It opens with "Starting in C#": a new page setting Python beside C#, plus three new lessons shared with PDP (compiler-errors, types-and-their-sizes, reading-input). A learner who did PDP in C# starts at "Classes and objects".
- **New C# pages in FOOP:** virtual-and-override, many-classes-one-promise (interfaces), two-names-one-object (struct against class), and namespaces-and-libraries.
- **Ids:** dewlab ids are kept where the topic maps. Three are renamed: powers-in-csharp (matching the draft already in drafts/lessons), dividing-in-csharp, and grids-and-references (C# has no comprehensions). No dewlab PDP or FOOP page is dropped. Maths-only sections are cut. a-polynomial-class moves to FOOP's extras.
- **Extras:** 14 in all, with reasons. 10 are picked from other dewlab courses; one is dewlab's own FOOP page (a-polynomial-class); three are new C# pages (the-game-of-life, a-deck-of-cards, asking-a-list-a-question).
- **Practice:** every tutorial-shaped lesson gets a practice page (32), plus one mixed set per series.
- **Batches 0 to 14:** first-steps and objects-and-classes are the batch 0 exemplars. A batch depends only on earlier ones, except that a tutorial and its practice page are written together. The extras come last.
- **Teacher notes** for each course cover what the page can't do, what goes to Visual Studio, how learners submit work, and which lessons each skills demonstration and the exam draw on.

**Checked, not guessed.** I checked every C# behaviour and compiler code the map states against the local .NET 10 SDK, in a scratch project outside the repo. Examples: -7 % 3 is -1; int.MaxValue + 1 goes round; double.Parse("12,50") gives 1250 under en-IE; the codes CS0193, CS0266, CS0019, CS0131, CS0029, CS0103, CS0161, CS0200, CS0815, CS0122, CS0176, CS0108, CS0114, CS0535, CS0163, CS1612, CS8421, CS5001, CS0017 and CS0246; local methods can be called before they are declared.

**Other work that changed my plan.** Mid-task the style guide was rewritten, and then given defaults. I followed them:
- At most two worlds on a page, so FOOP uses the game and the solar system plus your own, and three ocean-taught pages are retold (DECISIONS 13).
- `var` on "FOOP's second page", which I read as the-moves-you-already-know.
- The classic Main shown once, on the-tools-around-your-code.

I did not edit the style guide; the open questions flag the wording. The lesson data lives in one generator script in the scratchpad, so the map, the course files and the list below agree. I cross-checked that all 64 lesson ids match between the map and the course files.

lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO8, PDP-LO2. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. Recursion is in the maths module's algorithms (MIT-6.8) and in Computational Methods, and PDP's pages leave it out. A folder tree, folders inside folders, is the clearest reason for it.

lessons.title: Bits that flip: XOR and parity
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO4. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. C#'s `^` is the exclusive or that `powers-in-csharp` found by accident. Hiding a message with XOR, and catching a flipped bit with a parity bit, are small programs with a real use.

lessons.title: Random numbers: seeds and surprises you can repeat
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO10. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. Every game on these pages uses `Random`. `new Random(42)` gives the same numbers every run, which is how a game with chance in it can be tested.

lessons.title: The Monty Hall problem: three doors and a simulation
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO2, PDP-LO7. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. Almost everyone doubts the answer, and 10,000 games in a loop settle it. It needs only `Random`, `if` and loops.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo: estimating π with random darts
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO2. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. π from random numbers is a result people remember. The estimate settles as the darts go up, and a table of lines shows it without a chart.

lessons.title: Making change: three ways to use the fewest coins
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO2, PDP-LO8. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. Euro coins make it familiar. The greedy way fails for coins of 1, 3 and 4, a surprise worth an evening, and remembering answers in a `Dictionary` makes the slow way fast.

lessons.title: Markov chains: a dictionary that writes like a book
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO4, PDP-LO7. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. A dictionary of dictionaries, built from a real book, writes new sentences in the book's voice. Few exercises show as well what a `Dictionary` can do.

lessons.title: The Game of Life: a grid that changes by itself
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO7, PDP-LO8. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. Four rules on a grid of cells give patterns that move and grow, and surprise the person who wrote them. It needs only grids, loops and methods, and `Console.Clear()` works on the page.

lessons.title: Many languages, one idea: the same job in five languages
lessons.notes: Covers PDP-LO3. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. PDP-LO3 asks learners to tell languages apart, and the theory exam asks about it. The same job in C#, Python, SQL, JavaScript and BASIC, read side by side, gives something concrete to compare.

lessons.title: A polynomial class: a project in many methods
lessons.notes: Covers FOOP-LO4, FOOP-LO8. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. dewlab's FOOP lists it, but no outcome needs it beyond the other pages, and its lead-in is a maths page dewsharp does not have. In C# it gains operator overloading (`p + q`), which makes it a good extra.

lessons.title: A deck of cards: enums, a class and a shuffle
lessons.notes: Covers FOOP-LO1, FOOP-LO3, FOOP-LO7. Worlds: game. Size M. Explore. `Suit` and `Rank` are the enums every C# book uses, for good reason. A `Deck` that shuffles and deals, and a hand sorted through `IComparable`, end in a card game of the reader's own.

lessons.title: LINQ: asking a list a question
lessons.notes: Covers FOOP-LO4, FOOP-LO8. Worlds: game, solar system. Size M. Explore. PDP drops the comprehension because C# has none; LINQ is C#'s nearest relation, and it is part of the class library FOOP asks learners to use. Readers who liked comprehensions in Python meet the C# way here.

lessons.title: Simulating a queue: how busy is too busy?
lessons.notes: Covers FOOP-LO6, FOOP-LO7, FOOP-LO8. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. A `Customer` class and .NET's `Queue<T>` simulate a till; the wait grows without limit as the till nears full use, a result worth seeing. It uses a collection class, which FOOP names.

lessons.title: The perceptron: a class that learns from its mistakes
lessons.notes: Covers FOOP-LO3, FOOP-LO7. Worlds: none. Size M. Explore. A `Perceptron` class learns to tell two pixel shapes apart, drawn in `#` and `.`. Its fields change as it trains, which makes an object feel alive. It is long, so it is the last extra.

open_questions: The style guide counts FOOP's pages ('var on FOOP's second page'; 'instance before FOOP's third page'). FOOP now opens with 'Starting in C#', which is shared with PDP and writes every type. So the map counts from objects-and-classes, and the-moves-you-already-know teaches var. Should the style guide name the lessons instead? I did not edit it.

Should LESSON_FORMAT gain {{include: <file>}} for types cells? FOOP's class chain copies each world's class onto the next page, where dewlab keeps each version once in setup/oop/. Until it does, nothing catches a copy that has drifted.

How do tests work without tests: cells or assert? The map has the page write a small Check method (on building-reusable-tools and testing-what-a-class-does). The other choices are Debug.Assert (only if the page compiles with DEBUG defined, which is unknown) or a test helper the page provides. Its wording must not be a verdict.
LESSON_FORMAT's course file has no mixed: key, so the draft course files list each mixed set last in its series. Add a mixed: key as dewlab has?

Should PDP use lambdas? Sorting by a key (putting-things-in-order) and the paradigms on how-we-got-here pass a method to a method. Show it once as code to read, or leave it all to the extra asking-a-list-a-question?

Links to lessons not written yet: the batch rules make a later batch add forward links. Should the checker instead accept a lesson: link to any id that a course file lists, and show it as plain text until the lesson exists?
How is a number that appears only in an answer fold run? The powers-in-csharp draft's NOTES.md raises this. Options: a probe cell in the lesson's notes, or a hidden cell.
Private field naming: _fuel (usual in .NET) or fuel? The style guide doesn't say, and keeping-details-inside-an-object needs the answer.

What does the page show for an exception (the order of frames, the file and line)? .NET's own report lists the innermost call first, the reverse of a Python traceback. The prose on reading-an-error-message, when-it-goes-wrong and the-tools-around-your-code depends on it.

Two engine questions for the extras. What does the page do when a recursion never stops? That is a StackOverflow, which ends the .NET process and can't be caught (a-function-that-calls-itself). And does Thread.Sleep work on the page, for an animated the-game-of-life?
Which Visual Studio version does the college use, and do learners have Windows? Windows Forms, on a-front-end-for-a-class, needs Windows.
compiler-errors is fourth in PDP, not 'Lesson 1' as in the synthesis, so that the reader has types to get wrong first. first-steps meets one error and names compiling. Confirm.
FOOP's two worlds are the game and the solar system (DECISIONS 13), and the three ocean-taught pages are retold. Josh may prefer the ocean.

Rule 5 ('Main stays in its cell') needs a cell with a Main on the first page with classes (building-reusable-tools in PDP, objects-and-classes in FOOP). But the style guide shows the classic Main once, on a FOOP page. The map reads 'once' as the template's form (class Program with string[] args), on the-tools-around-your-code. Confirm, or move rule 5's cell.
